options.explanation: Read visibility does not enlist another system.

options.label: To disable offset commits
options.explanation: Position management remains available.

options.label: To hide records from aborted producer transactions
options.explanation: The consumer returns only transactional data whose commit marker makes it visible.

stem: What can a Kafka producer transaction atomically include?

options.label: Writes to multiple Kafka partitions plus consumed-offset commits
options.explanation: Transactions coordinate Kafka records and group offsets for read-process-write pipelines.

options.label: An arbitrary SQL commit at another vendor
options.explanation: Kafka cannot atomically control an external database transaction.

options.label: Every consumer’s future side effects
options.explanation: Downstream processing remains independently executed.

options.label: A broker software upgrade
options.explanation: Operational lifecycle is outside record transactions.

stem: Why must a Kafka transactional.id be stable for one logical producer across restarts?

options.label: It chooses the consumer group rebalance leader
options.explanation: Transactional producer identity does not assign consumers.

options.label: The coordinator can fence an older producer incarnation
options.explanation: Stable identity lets a newer epoch prevent zombie instances from committing.

options.label: It encrypts transaction records
options.explanation: The identifier coordinates epochs and carries no encryption key.

options.label: It makes all topics one partition
options.explanation: Transaction scope does not change partition topology.

stem: What is a zombie producer in transactional messaging?

options.label: A consumer that reads a tombstone
options.explanation: Compacted-log deletion markers are valid records, not zombie producers.

options.label: A broker outside the ISR
options.explanation: Replica synchronization is a different role.

options.label: An old instance that resumes and tries to write after replacement
options.explanation: Fencing prevents stale ownership from committing conflicting output.

options.label: A permanently malformed message
options.explanation: Poison-message handling concerns consumer retries.

stem: Why does Kafka exactly-once stream processing not imply exactly-once email sending?

options.label: Emails cannot contain event IDs
options.explanation: Applications can include identity, but the external effect still needs coordination.

options.label: Kafka transactions do not support partitions
options.explanation: They can span multiple Kafka partitions.

options.label: Consumers cannot read committed data
options.explanation: Read-committed isolation is explicitly available.

options.label: The email provider is outside the Kafka transaction boundary
options.explanation: Atomic Kafka writes and offsets cannot roll back or deduplicate an external send.

stem: Without idempotence, how can multiple in-flight produce requests plus retry reorder records?

options.label: A later batch succeeds before an earlier failed batch is retried
options.explanation: Independent outstanding requests can complete in a different sequence after failure.

options.label: The broker sorts record values alphabetically
options.explanation: Kafka appends accepted batches rather than sorting payloads.

options.label: Consumer commits rewrite the log
options.explanation: Offset commits do not mutate record order.

options.label: Replication reverses every batch
options.explanation: Follower copying preserves leader log order.

stem: A topic has replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2, and only one ISR member. What happens to an acks=all write?

options.label: It succeeds because one leader is enough
options.explanation: That behavior would defeat min.insync.replicas.

options.label: It is rejected for insufficient in-sync replicas
options.explanation: Only one synchronized copy cannot satisfy the configured minimum of two.

options.label: It waits for all three consumers
options.explanation: Broker replicas, not consumers, determine this write condition.

options.label: It is silently stored only on the producer
options.explanation: Producer memory is not a committed broker log.

stem: Why are replication factor and current ISR size different?

options.label: ISR counts consumer groups instead of brokers
options.explanation: ISR contains partition replicas.

options.label: Replication factor changes on every message
options.explanation: Assignment remains stable until administrative reassignment.

options.label: Assigned replicas can exist but temporarily fall out of sync
options.explanation: Replication factor is topology intent; ISR reflects replicas currently meeting synchronization criteria.

options.label: They differ only when schemas are invalid
options.explanation: Payload validation does not define replica health.

stem: What is the goal of cooperative incremental rebalancing?

options.label: Give one consumer every partition permanently
options.explanation: The protocol still adapts ownership to group membership.

options.label: Remove the need to commit offsets
options.explanation: Transferred partitions still need safe progress handoff.

options.label: Create global ordering across topics
options.explanation: Assignment strategy cannot merge independent logs.

options.label: Move only necessary partitions while others continue processing
options.explanation: Incremental revocation reduces the stop-the-world disruption of eager reassignment.

stem: How can static consumer membership reduce avoidable rebalances?

options.label: A restarting instance can reclaim its identity within the session window
options.explanation: Stable membership avoids treating brief restarts as permanent group replacement.

options.label: It prevents all process failures
options.explanation: Identity does not improve host reliability.

options.label: It disables partition reassignment forever
options.explanation: True membership changes still require redistribution.

options.label: It commits records before processing
options.explanation: Membership has no such offset policy.

stem: What should a consumer do when partitions are revoked during rebalance?

options.label: Continue processing indefinitely after revocation
options.explanation: The new owner may start, creating conflicting concurrent effects.

options.label: Stop new work and safely checkpoint completed progress for those partitions
options.explanation: A clean handoff prevents concurrent ownership and limits replay.

options.label: Delete the underlying partition log
options.explanation: Consumers do not own broker retention.

options.label: Reset offsets to zero unconditionally
options.explanation: Forced full replay is neither required nor safe by default.

stem: Why can “10,000 records of lag” be a misleading cross-topic comparison?

options.label: Offsets are measured only in bytes
options.explanation: Offsets identify record positions, although record sizes still vary.

options.label: Lag cannot be monitored per partition
options.explanation: Kafka exposes positional progress at partition scope.

options.label: Record sizes and production rates determine how much time and work lag represents
options.explanation: The same count can mean milliseconds on one stream and hours on another.

options.label: Every topic produces at the same rate
options.explanation: Workloads commonly differ substantially.

stem: A window result was emitted before a late event arrived. What output capability preserves correctness?

options.label: Rewrite the already delivered network packet
options.explanation: Past deliveries cannot be mutated in transit.

options.label: Change the source event timestamp
options.explanation: Consumers must not falsify original occurrence time.

options.label: Ignore every late event regardless of policy
options.explanation: That trades away completeness rather than preserving it.

options.label: Emit an update or retraction for the prior result
options.explanation: Downstream consumers need a correction when the aggregate changes after initial publication.

sources.title: RabbitMQ Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms

stem: What is dangerous about acknowledging multiple deliveries up to a tag before all are durably processed?

options.label: One bulk ack can discard responsibility for unfinished earlier deliveries
options.explanation: The broker treats the entire acknowledged range as complete.

options.label: It creates more queue replicas
options.explanation: Acknowledgement range does not alter topology.

options.label: It forces each message into a DLQ
options.explanation: Positive acknowledgement removes normal deliveries.

options.label: It prevents publisher confirms
options.explanation: Consumer and publisher confirmation channels are independent.

stem: For a persistent message in a RabbitMQ quorum queue, when is publisher confirmation meaningful?

options.label: After every consumer finishes its side effect
options.explanation: Publisher confirmation precedes arbitrary downstream business handling.

options.label: After a quorum has accepted the message under the queue protocol
options.explanation: The confirm reflects replicated broker responsibility rather than merely a socket write.

options.label: As soon as the client serializes the payload
options.explanation: Local serialization provides no broker durability.

options.label: Only after the message retention period ends
options.explanation: Confirmation supports immediate producer progress.

stem: Why can ordinary dead-letter republishing lose a message in some RabbitMQ configurations?

options.label: Dead-letter messages never use exchanges
options.explanation: They are republished through an exchange.

options.label: A nack always deletes the entire queue
options.explanation: Rejection changes one or a range of deliveries.

options.label: The source can remove it without confirmed acceptance by the DLX target
options.explanation: A failed internal republish leaves no copy unless at-least-once dead-lettering is configured.

options.label: Quorum queues cannot have dead-letter policies
options.explanation: They support dead-lettering with additional safety options.

stem: How should a high-throughput publisher use confirms without blocking after every message?

options.label: Ignore every negative confirm
options.explanation: A nack indicates publication uncertainty or failure that requires handling.

options.label: Reuse one message ID for the entire window
options.explanation: Distinct logical events need distinct identity for recovery.

options.label: Wait for consumer acknowledgements on the publish channel
options.explanation: Consumer completion is not reported as publisher confirms.

options.label: Track a bounded window of outstanding sequence numbers and handle async confirms
options.explanation: Pipelining retains broker acceptance evidence while amortizing round trips.

stem: A JetStream message is redelivered after AckWait, then the first worker’s late ack arrives. What implication matters?

options.label: Two workers may have executed, so side effects still need idempotency
options.explanation: Broker acknowledgement state cannot undo a duplicate external action already in flight.

options.label: The stream guarantees only the second worker ran
options.explanation: Timeout redelivery occurs precisely while first-worker outcome is uncertain.

options.label: The late ack changes the event payload
options.explanation: Acknowledgements alter delivery state, not content.

options.label: MaxAckPending becomes a retention policy
options.explanation: Flow control remains separate from stream retention.

stem: What does JetStream double acknowledgement strengthen?

options.label: Atomicity of an external database write and acknowledgement
options.explanation: A broker ack round trip cannot enlist arbitrary storage.

options.label: Certainty that the server recorded the consumer acknowledgement
options.explanation: The consumer waits for confirmation of ack receipt, closing one redelivery ambiguity.

options.label: Ordering among different subjects
options.explanation: Acknowledgement confirmation does not impose a global order.

options.label: Durability of Core NATS messages
options.explanation: The mechanism belongs to JetStream consumer state.

stem: In AMQP link credit, what does a receiver grant to a sender?

options.label: Ownership of the receiver’s database
options.explanation: Link flow has no access-control transfer to application storage.

options.label: A guarantee that all deliveries are accepted
options.explanation: Disposition can still reject or release transferred messages.

options.label: Permission to transfer a bounded number of deliveries
options.explanation: Credit is protocol-level flow control expressing receiver capacity.

options.label: An infinite retention period
options.explanation: Credit governs in-flight transfer, not broker storage lifetime.

stem: Why must an exactly-once broker feature be read with its scope and failure assumptions?

options.label: Exactly-once is a universal property of HTTP
options.explanation: Delivery products define explicit boundaries; transports do not confer it globally.

options.label: Scope matters only for message size
options.explanation: Geography, subscriptions, and acknowledgements can bound semantics.

options.label: External databases automatically join broker commits
options.explanation: Independent systems require their own atomicity or idempotency design.

options.label: The guarantee may cover delivery acknowledgement but not external effects or all regions
options.explanation: Application correctness extends beyond the broker’s defined protocol boundary.

stem: Why is deduplication by transient delivery-attempt ID weaker than by immutable event ID?

options.label: Redeliveries can receive new attempt identities for one logical event
options.explanation: A stable producer identity is needed to correlate all attempts.

options.label: Attempt IDs are always cryptographic secrets
options.explanation: Their uniqueness does not make them an authentication credential.

options.label: Event IDs prevent all producer bugs
options.explanation: Stable identity helps detect repeats but cannot validate arbitrary event correctness.

options.label: Delivery attempts never cross consumers
options.explanation: Retries commonly move between workers.

stem: Why can attaching a DLQ be problematic for a workflow that requires strict FIFO completion?

options.label: A DLQ always duplicates every healthy message
options.explanation: Only failed or expired deliveries are normally redirected.

options.label: Removing a failed item lets later items advance ahead of it
options.explanation: Dead-letter isolation improves liveness by breaking the original completion order.

options.label: FIFO queues cannot retry
options.explanation: They support retries but ordering interacts with poison messages.

options.label: Dead-letter retention is infinite
options.explanation: DLQs have configurable retention.

stem: How can a webhook receiver avoid acknowledging an event that might be lost before processing?

options.label: Return success before signature verification
options.explanation: That accepts untrusted data and suppresses legitimate retries.

options.label: Hold the HTTP connection until every downstream completes
options.explanation: Long synchronous chains increase timeout and redelivery risk.

options.label: Persist the event or inbox record durably before returning success
options.explanation: Durable acceptance transfers responsibility safely, after which workers can retry locally.

options.label: Store only the provider IP address
options.explanation: Connection metadata cannot reconstruct the event.

stem: How can a receiver rotate webhook signing secrets without dropping valid deliveries?

options.label: Disable verification until all retries finish
options.explanation: That opens an impersonation window.

options.label: Rewrite stored payloads with the new secret
options.explanation: Signatures cover original bytes and cannot be repaired by mutation.

options.label: Treat every failed signature as a retryable 500
options.explanation: Authentication failures should not create an unbounded attacker-controlled retry loop.

options.label: Accept signatures from old and new secrets during a bounded overlap
options.explanation: Dual verification supports in-flight deliveries while senders transition.

stem: Which metric type should record the cumulative number of HTTP requests handled by a process?

options.label: A counter named http_requests_total
options.explanation: Correct — Counters represent monotonically increasing totals, and Prometheus convention uses the _total suffix.

options.label: A gauge named http_requests_current
options.explanation: Incorrect — A gauge represents a value that can rise and fall, not a cumulative event total.

options.label: A histogram named http_requests_info
options.explanation: Incorrect — Histograms aggregate observations into buckets rather than storing one event total.

options.label: A log line emitted only at shutdown
options.explanation: Incorrect — A shutdown-only log cannot provide a continuously queryable cumulative time series.

stem: A worker queue grows and shrinks throughout the day. Which metric type fits its current depth?

options.label: A counter
options.explanation: Incorrect — Counters cannot decrease except through process reset, so they misrepresent queue drainage.

options.label: A gauge
options.explanation: Correct — Gauges model instantaneous values that legitimately increase and decrease over time.

options.label: A cumulative histogram
options.explanation: Incorrect — A histogram records distributions of observations rather than one current queue size.

options.label: A trace span count stored as text
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace spans describe operations and are inefficient for the current aggregate depth.

stem: You need fleet-wide p95 request latency aggregated across instances. Which Prometheus metric is suitable?

options.label: A counter containing the last latency
options.explanation: Incorrect — A counter must be monotonic and cannot represent individual latency observations.

options.label: A gauge containing each instance p95
options.explanation: Incorrect — Averaging per-instance quantiles does not produce the global request quantile.

options.label: A histogram with shared bucket boundaries
options.explanation: Correct — Histogram buckets can be summed across instances and used to estimate fleet-wide quantiles.

options.label: A client-side summary from each instance
options.explanation: Incorrect — Summary quantiles generally cannot be meaningfully averaged or aggregated across instances.

stem: Why is user_id usually a bad Prometheus metric label?

options.label: Labels are visible only in traces
options.explanation: Incorrect — Metric labels are fundamental dimensions in the metrics backend itself.

options.label: Labels may contain only integers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Prometheus label values are strings and are not restricted to numeric values.

options.label: User IDs prevent counters from increasing
options.explanation: Incorrect — Counter behavior is independent of whether a label value identifies a user.

options.label: It creates an unbounded number of time series
options.explanation: Correct — Every distinct label set becomes a series, so user identifiers can exhaust memory and storage.

stem: A request is rejected because the caller supplied invalid input. Which logging choice is usually most useful?

options.label: A structured warning or informational event with validation context, not a stack trace
options.explanation: Correct — Expected client errors should be queryable without implying an internal crash or flooding logs with stacks.

options.label: A fatal event that terminates the server
options.explanation: Incorrect — A single invalid request is not a process-wide unrecoverable condition.

options.label: No event under any circumstances
options.explanation: Incorrect — Aggregated validation failures can reveal client regressions or abuse and can be useful when sampled appropriately.

options.label: The full request including passwords and tokens
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sensitive credentials must not be recorded merely to add debugging context.

stem: What does one distributed-trace span represent?

options.label: The current value of every host metric
options.explanation: Incorrect — Host metric snapshots are measurements, not the semantic unit of a trace.

options.label: A timed operation with context, attributes, events, and links
options.explanation: Correct — A span is the fundamental trace unit describing work performed during an interval.

options.label: An immutable copy of all application logs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Logs may correlate with spans but are distinct telemetry records.

options.label: A complete incident timeline written by responders
options.explanation: Incorrect — An incident timeline is human coordination data rather than one instrumented operation.

stem: Service A calls Service B synchronously during one request. How should their server spans normally relate?

options.label: B’s span becomes the parent of A’s span
options.explanation: Incorrect — The caller initiates the downstream operation, so reversing ancestry misstates causality.

options.label: The spans must share the same span ID
options.explanation: Incorrect — Every span has its own identifier; trace ID is the shared trace identity.

options.label: B’s server span is a child of A’s client span
options.explanation: Correct — Parent-child context expresses the causal nested RPC operation in the distributed trace.

options.label: Both spans start unrelated traces
options.explanation: Incorrect — Discarding propagated context prevents end-to-end causal reconstruction.

stem: What does the W3C traceparent header propagate between services?

options.label: The caller’s authentication token
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace context is observability metadata and must not replace request authentication.

options.label: The complete list of every prior span
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace history remains in telemetry storage and is not serialized into each request header.

options.label: All metric label values from the caller
options.explanation: Incorrect — Metric dimensions are not transported through traceparent.

options.label: Trace identity, parent span identity, version, and trace flags
options.explanation: Correct — Traceparent carries the minimal standardized fields needed to continue a distributed trace.

stem: Why prefer structured fields such as request_id and status_code over embedding everything in one message string?

options.label: Machines can filter and aggregate stable fields without fragile text parsing
options.explanation: Correct — Structured log attributes preserve typed or named dimensions for reliable queries and correlation.

options.label: Structured logs guarantee smaller files
options.explanation: Incorrect — Field names and serialization can increase size, so compactness is not guaranteed.

options.label: They automatically redact all secrets
options.explanation: Incorrect — Redaction still requires explicit policy and instrumentation.

options.label: They replace metrics and traces entirely
options.explanation: Incorrect — Each telemetry signal answers different questions and remains useful alongside logs.

sources.title: RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet

stem: Which timestamp is most interoperable for a structured event crossing time zones?

options.label: Thursday morning
options.explanation: Incorrect — Natural language is locale-dependent and lacks an exact instant.

options.label: An RFC 3339 timestamp with an explicit UTC offset, such as 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z
options.explanation: Correct — The format supplies an unambiguous date, time, and offset for machine exchange.

options.label: 10:00 with no offset or date
options.explanation: Incorrect — The value is ambiguous across dates, zones, and daylight-saving transitions.

options.label: A server-local formatted string without zone
options.explanation: Incorrect — Consumers cannot reliably order events from hosts in different zones.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: What is a service-level indicator?

options.label: The target percentage the team intends to meet
options.explanation: Incorrect — The target for an SLI is the SLO, not the indicator itself.

options.label: A list of every monitoring dashboard
options.explanation: Incorrect — Dashboards visualize data but do not define one reliability measurement.

options.label: A quantitative measure of some aspect of service behavior
options.explanation: Correct — An SLI is the measured signal, such as successful request proportion or latency compliance.

options.label: A contractual consequence for missing a target
options.explanation: Incorrect — Contractual consequences belong to an SLA rather than the measured indicator.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: A team states that 99.9% of eligible requests should succeed over 28 days. What is this?

options.label: A capacity limit
options.explanation: Incorrect — The objective is user-visible success, not an infrastructure resource ceiling.

options.label: A service-level indicator
options.explanation: Incorrect — The indicator would be the observed success ratio, without the target requirement.

options.label: A trace sampling rule
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling controls telemetry collection and does not state the reliability target.

options.label: A service-level objective
options.explanation: Correct — It sets a target value for an explicitly measured indicator over a defined window.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: For a 99.9% availability SLO, what does the remaining 0.1% represent?

options.label: The error budget for tolerated unreliability during the window
options.explanation: Correct — The complement of the objective quantifies how much bad service can occur before the SLO is missed.

options.label: The percentage of traffic that must be traced
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace sampling is independent of the acceptable service error ratio.

options.label: A mandatory CPU idle reserve
options.explanation: Incorrect — Capacity headroom can support reliability but is not mathematically the SLO complement.

options.label: The fraction of alerts responders may ignore
options.explanation: Incorrect — Alerts require action based on impact and policy, not a blanket ignore allowance.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: Which set is known as the four golden signals for monitoring a service?

options.label: CPU, RAM, disk, and operating system
options.explanation: Incorrect — Those are host components and omit direct user-visible behavior.

options.label: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation
options.explanation: Correct — These signals cover response time, demand, failures, and resource pressure.

options.label: Logs, metrics, traces, and profiles
options.explanation: Incorrect — Those are telemetry signal types rather than the four service-health signals.

options.label: Build, test, deploy, and rollback
options.explanation: Incorrect — Those are delivery lifecycle activities, not runtime monitoring signals.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: Which alert best reflects a user-visible symptom?

options.label: A deployment occurred ten minutes ago
options.explanation: Incorrect — A change is diagnostic context, not itself a service symptom.

options.label: The log file grew by 2 GB
options.explanation: Incorrect — Log volume may need attention but does not directly measure checkout experience.

options.label: Checkout success rate is below its SLO threshold
options.explanation: Correct — Failed checkouts directly measure whether users receive the intended service.

options.label: One host has 72% CPU utilization
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU may be healthy or unhealthy depending on workload and does not prove user impact.

sources.title: Kubernetes: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

stem: A pod is alive but temporarily cannot serve traffic while warming its cache. Which Kubernetes probe should fail?

options.label: Every probe must succeed because the process exists
options.explanation: Incorrect — Process existence does not mean the application is ready to receive requests.

options.label: The liveness probe
options.explanation: Incorrect — Liveness failure triggers restart and is inappropriate for a temporary traffic-readiness condition.

options.label: The startup probe after startup completed
options.explanation: Incorrect — Startup probes protect slow initialization and stop running after success.

options.label: The readiness probe
options.explanation: Correct — Readiness removes the pod from service endpoints without necessarily restarting it.

sources.title: Kubernetes: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

stem: A process is permanently deadlocked and cannot recover without restart. Which probe is intended to detect this?

options.label: The liveness probe
options.explanation: Correct — Repeated liveness failure tells Kubernetes to restart a container that is no longer making progress.

options.label: The readiness probe only
options.explanation: Incorrect — Readiness can stop traffic but does not by itself restart the deadlocked process.

options.label: A PodDisruptionBudget
options.explanation: Incorrect — A disruption budget controls voluntary eviction availability, not application health detection.

options.label: A CPU request
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resource requests influence scheduling and do not identify a deadlock.

sources.title: Kubernetes: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

stem: Why configure a startup probe for an application with a slow, variable initialization?

options.label: It permanently disables liveness checks
options.explanation: Incorrect — After startup succeeds, configured liveness and readiness probes take over.

options.label: It delays liveness and readiness enforcement until startup succeeds
options.explanation: Correct — The startup probe prevents premature restarts while still allowing strict runtime liveness thresholds.

options.label: It reserves additional CPU automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect — Probe configuration does not alter container resource requests or limits.

options.label: It guarantees dependencies are highly available
options.explanation: Incorrect — It observes this container’s startup and cannot guarantee external systems.

stem: During a major incident, what is the incident commander’s primary role?

options.label: Write the final postmortem before mitigation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Restoring service and maintaining situational awareness take precedence during the active incident.

options.label: Approve all future production releases
options.explanation: Incorrect — Long-term release governance is not the operational command role in one incident.

options.label: Coordinate the response, assign roles, and maintain overall decision flow
options.explanation: Correct — Clear command prevents duplicated work and lets technical responders focus on investigation and mitigation.

options.label: Personally debug every failing component
options.explanation: Incorrect — One person cannot effectively coordinate while owning every technical thread.

stem: Why assign a dedicated communications lead during a large incident?

options.label: To decide database repair commands alone
options.explanation: Incorrect — Technical remediation remains with qualified operations roles and review procedures.

options.label: To hide uncertainty until the incident ends
options.explanation: Incorrect — Useful updates can state uncertainty honestly and should not wait for complete knowledge.

options.label: To replace the incident commander
options.explanation: Incorrect — Communication is a distinct role operating under the response structure.

options.label: To provide consistent stakeholder updates without interrupting technical responders
options.explanation: Correct — Separating communication reduces context switching and prevents contradictory external messages.

stem: What does “blameless” mean in an incident postmortem?

options.label: Analyze actions in their system context to improve defenses rather than punish individuals
options.explanation: Correct — Blameless inquiry encourages accurate disclosure of contributing conditions and durable corrective work.

options.label: Conclude that nobody made a mistake
options.explanation: Incorrect — Human actions can be mistaken; the point is to understand why they were reasonable in context.

options.label: Avoid naming failed controls or decisions
options.explanation: Incorrect — A useful postmortem is specific about mechanisms and choices while avoiding personal punishment.

options.label: Exclude human actions from the timeline
options.explanation: Incorrect — Operator decisions are important evidence and should be analyzed contextually.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: Contingency Planning Guide

stem: What does a recovery time objective constrain?

options.label: The maximum amount of data loss measured in time
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is the recovery point objective rather than restoration duration.

options.label: The target maximum time to restore service after disruption
options.explanation: Correct — RTO expresses how quickly recovery should complete following an outage.

options.label: The request latency percentile during normal operation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Steady-state latency belongs to a service objective, not disaster recovery time.

options.label: The age of retained log files
options.explanation: Incorrect — Log retention may support investigations but is not the RTO definition.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: Contingency Planning Guide

stem: What does a recovery point objective constrain?

options.label: How long responders remain on call
options.explanation: Incorrect — Staffing shifts are operational policy rather than data-loss tolerance.

options.label: The number of replicas in steady state
options.explanation: Incorrect — Replica count can influence RPO but is not the objective itself.

options.label: The maximum acceptable data-loss interval after recovery
options.explanation: Correct — RPO determines how far back restored data may be relative to the failure.

options.label: How quickly service must be restored
options.explanation: Incorrect — Restoration duration is governed by RTO.

stem: Why shed excess load before a service is completely saturated?

options.label: It removes the need for capacity planning
options.explanation: Incorrect — Capacity and demand forecasting remain necessary despite overload protection.

options.label: It guarantees every request eventually succeeds
options.explanation: Incorrect — Shedding explicitly rejects some requests to protect overall health.

options.label: It increases queue length to smooth demand
options.explanation: Incorrect — Effective shedding limits admitted work rather than building an unbounded queue.

options.label: Rejecting some work quickly can preserve useful service for the rest
options.explanation: Correct — Controlled admission prevents queue growth and resource exhaustion from turning overload into total failure.

stem: Why operate a latency-sensitive service with capacity headroom?

options.label: Traffic bursts and failures can be absorbed before saturation causes nonlinear latency
options.explanation: Correct — Spare capacity gives the system room to handle variance and reduced capacity during maintenance or failure.

options.label: Idle resources make every request free
options.explanation: Incorrect — Infrastructure cost remains even when capacity is unused.

options.label: Headroom replaces redundancy
options.explanation: Incorrect — Spare capacity and fault-domain redundancy solve related but distinct failure modes.

options.label: It forces all hosts to run at identical utilization
options.explanation: Incorrect — Load distribution can vary while the fleet still maintains sufficient aggregate reserve.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: Why can immediate retries worsen an overloaded dependency?

options.label: Retries always bypass authentication
options.explanation: Incorrect — Authentication handling is unrelated to the overload amplification mechanism.

options.label: They multiply offered load while the dependency has the least spare capacity
options.explanation: Correct — Retries consume more queues, connections, and compute, creating positive feedback during failure.

options.label: They convert all requests into cache hits
options.explanation: Incorrect — Retries usually repeat dependency work and do not inherently populate or use caches.

options.label: They make network latency exactly zero
options.explanation: Incorrect — Additional attempts add load and latency rather than eliminate them.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: What is the purpose of exponential backoff between retries?

options.label: Make a non-idempotent operation idempotent
options.explanation: Incorrect — Retry timing does not provide duplicate suppression.

options.label: Preserve strict request ordering across clients
options.explanation: Incorrect — Independent randomized schedules do not establish a global order.

options.label: Reduce repeated pressure by increasing the delay after consecutive failures
options.explanation: Correct — Longer delays give a struggling dependency time to recover and reduce synchronized retry traffic.

options.label: Guarantee the next attempt will succeed
options.explanation: Incorrect — Backoff changes timing but cannot guarantee recovery.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: Why add jitter to retry backoff?

options.label: To make failed requests safe methods
options.explanation: Incorrect — HTTP method semantics do not change with scheduling randomness.

options.label: To increase the maximum number of attempts
options.explanation: Incorrect — Jitter changes timing distribution, not necessarily retry count.

options.label: To encrypt retry timestamps
options.explanation: Incorrect — Random delay is not a confidentiality mechanism.

options.label: To prevent many clients from retrying at the same deterministic instants
options.explanation: Correct — Random variation spreads attempts over time and reduces synchronized load spikes.

stem: What is the core purpose of a canary release?

options.label: Expose a small representative traffic slice before broad rollout
options.explanation: Correct — Limited exposure provides production evidence while bounding the impact of a bad version.

options.label: Deploy to every instance simultaneously
options.explanation: Incorrect — Fleet-wide rollout eliminates the limited blast-radius property.

options.label: Run only unit tests in a developer laptop
options.explanation: Incorrect — A canary specifically evaluates behavior in a production-like serving environment.

options.label: Keep the old and new versions forever
options.explanation: Incorrect — Canarying is an evaluation stage leading to promotion or rollback.

stem: What does a Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget primarily constrain?

options.label: All involuntary failures such as hardware loss
options.explanation: Incorrect — A PDB cannot prevent node crashes or other involuntary disruptions.

options.label: The number of replicas unavailable during voluntary disruptions
options.explanation: Correct — A PDB protects application availability during actions such as node drain or voluntary eviction.

options.label: The maximum CPU consumed by each pod
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU limits and requests control resource allocation, not disruptions.

options.label: The number of requests an API client sends
options.explanation: Incorrect — Client request quotas are unrelated to pod eviction policy.

stem: A Prometheus process counter resets on restart. Which query concept estimates requests per second correctly?

options.label: Treat every lower value as negative traffic
options.explanation: Incorrect — A reset indicates a new process sequence, not negative requests.

options.label: Subtract the counter from a fixed maximum
options.explanation: Incorrect — Counters have no required maximum and this would invert meaning.

options.label: Compute rate over a range so counter resets are detected
options.explanation: Correct — Prometheus rate functions account for monotonic increases and adjust for observed resets.

options.label: Average the raw counter values across time
options.explanation: Incorrect — Averaging cumulative totals does not produce an event rate.

stem: A histogram reports le="0.5" = 80 and le="1" = 95. How many observations were between 0.5 and 1 second?

options.explanation: Incorrect — That includes every observation at or below one second, including the first bucket.
Incorrect — Adding cumulative buckets double-counts observations below 0.5 seconds.

options.label: The value cannot be inferred
options.explanation: Incorrect — With aligned cumulative buckets, the interval count is directly recoverable by subtraction.
Correct — Histogram buckets are cumulative, so subtracting 80 from 95 isolates the interval.

stem: A latency histogram has buckets at 100 ms and 1 s but the SLO threshold is 300 ms. What is the key limitation?

options.label: The data cannot precisely distinguish observations just below and above 300 ms
options.explanation: Correct — All observations between 100 ms and 1 s share one bucket, so interpolation can be very inaccurate.

options.label: Histograms cannot count requests
options.explanation: Incorrect — Histogram count and bucket series explicitly track observation counts.

options.label: The metric cannot be aggregated across instances
options.explanation: Incorrect — Histogram buckets with matching boundaries are designed for aggregation.

options.label: The server must emit every latency as a log
options.explanation: Incorrect — Better bucket placement solves the SLO-resolution problem without per-request logs.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: A target disappears from service discovery. Why is alerting only on its application error counter insufficient?

options.label: Service discovery emits every application exception
options.explanation: Incorrect — Discovery knows targets, not internal exception events.

options.label: No new samples may arrive, so absence itself must be detected
options.explanation: Correct — A vanished target cannot increment its own errors; monitoring needs up, expected-target, or missing-series checks.

options.label: Counters automatically become gauges when a host disappears
options.explanation: Incorrect — Metric type does not change based on scrape availability.

options.label: Application errors always reach zero before failure
options.explanation: Incorrect — A missing series is not equivalent to a healthy zero value.

stem: In the OpenTelemetry log data model, where should a machine-queryable HTTP status normally live?

options.label: Only inside SeverityText
options.explanation: Incorrect — SeverityText represents level names such as ERROR, not status dimensions.

options.label: Inside TraceId by encoding the number
options.explanation: Incorrect — TraceId has a fixed tracing identity role and cannot be repurposed.

options.label: In a named attribute, leaving Body for the main event message
options.explanation: Correct — Attributes hold structured event context while Body carries the primary human or structured payload.

options.label: In ObservedTimestamp with the status added
options.explanation: Incorrect — ObservedTimestamp records when telemetry observed the event, not HTTP outcome.

stem: A login failure contains a submitted password and session token. What should the logger record?

options.label: The entire Authorization header because storage is internal
options.explanation: Incorrect — Internal logs are widely accessible and often exported, so authorization data remains sensitive.

options.label: Nothing about authentication failures
options.explanation: Incorrect — Security monitoring needs safe event metadata such as account identifier policy, source, and result.

options.label: The plaintext password to reproduce the issue
options.explanation: Incorrect — Passwords must not become recoverable diagnostic data.

options.label: Useful event context with credentials excluded or irreversibly masked
options.explanation: Correct — Authentication events are valuable, but passwords and session identifiers can enable compromise if logged.

stem: An incoming traceparent has the sampled flag unset. What does that flag communicate?

options.label: The caller’s recording or sampling recommendation for this trace
options.explanation: Correct — Trace flags carry a propagated sampling decision, though local policy still governs behavior.

options.label: The service must erase all logs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace sampling does not mandate deletion of other telemetry signals.

options.label: The request must be rejected
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling metadata has no authorization or request-validity semantics.

options.label: The trace ID is invalid
options.explanation: Incorrect — A valid trace context can be unsampled.

stem: Why can head-based trace sampling miss rare failed requests?

options.label: Head sampling records only database spans
options.explanation: Incorrect — The strategy is about decision timing, not a particular span kind.

options.label: The keep/drop decision occurs before the final outcome is known
options.explanation: Correct — Early probability decisions cannot preferentially retain failures discovered later in the trace.

options.label: Failed spans have no trace IDs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Errors can be represented on ordinary identified spans.

options.label: It requires every trace to be retained
options.explanation: Incorrect — Head sampling deliberately drops some traces early.

stem: What is the main operational cost of tail-based trace sampling?

options.label: Applications cannot propagate trace context
options.explanation: Incorrect — Context propagation works independently of where sampling decisions finish.

options.label: Every trace is stored permanently
options.explanation: Incorrect — Tail samplers can discard traces after evaluation rather than retain all of them.

options.label: A collector must buffer trace data until enough of the outcome is known
options.explanation: Correct — Outcome-aware selection requires memory, coordination, and delayed export for distributed spans.

options.label: Metrics become mathematically invalid
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace sampling does not inherently alter separately aggregated application metrics.

stem: An HTTP server returns 404 for an expected missing resource. Should instrumentation automatically mark the span as an error?

options.label: Never, because HTTP status cannot influence span status
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unexpected protocol outcomes can and should be reflected according to semantic conventions.

options.label: Only if the trace ID ends in an odd digit
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling identity has no relationship to operation success.

options.label: Always, because every 4xx is a server failure
options.explanation: Incorrect — Many 4xx responses are expected client outcomes and do not indicate server malfunction.

options.label: Not necessarily; server span status depends on whether the outcome is an error for the application operation
options.explanation: Correct — Semantic conventions distinguish protocol status from application-level error meaning and allow expected outcomes.

stem: A single operation encounters a notable exception but performs no distinct nested unit of work. How can it record this?

options.label: Add an exception event to the current span
options.explanation: Correct — Events capture time-stamped annotations within a span without inventing a separate operation.

options.label: Store the exception as a metric label
options.explanation: Incorrect — Stack traces and messages are high-cardinality event data, not metric dimensions.

options.label: Create an unrelated root trace
options.explanation: Incorrect — Breaking trace context would lose the exception’s connection to the operation.

options.label: Change the trace ID after the exception
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace identity must remain stable throughout the distributed request.

stem: Why should personal data generally not be placed in propagated baggage?

options.label: Baggage values are guaranteed to be deleted at every hop
options.explanation: Incorrect — The purpose of baggage is propagation, so downstream services may receive it.

options.label: Baggage can cross service and trust boundaries and is not automatically encrypted or redacted
options.explanation: Correct — Propagation spreads values broadly, creating privacy exposure and header overhead.

options.label: Baggage supports numeric values only
options.explanation: Incorrect — Values are strings and can contain many data types after encoding.

options.label: Trace sampling fails whenever baggage exists
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling and baggage are separate context mechanisms.

stem: Why must a service treat incoming trace context as untrusted input?

options.label: Trace IDs are always executable code
options.explanation: Incorrect — They are identifiers, but malformed or attacker-controlled metadata still needs safe parsing.

options.label: Only authenticated users can send HTTP headers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Any network caller reaching the endpoint can generally supply tracing headers.

options.label: External callers can forge identifiers or flags, so values need validation and policy controls
options.explanation: Correct — Trace context crosses trust boundaries and can otherwise enable resource abuse or misleading correlation.

options.label: Valid trace context proves authorization
options.explanation: Incorrect — Observability correlation is not an identity or permission mechanism.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: Why must an SLO specify a measurement window?

options.label: The window determines TLS certificate validity
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificate lifetimes are independent of service-objective measurement.

options.label: It forces all incidents to last exactly that long
options.explanation: Incorrect — The window evaluates aggregate performance and does not prescribe outage duration.

options.label: Metrics cannot store timestamps
options.explanation: Incorrect — Time series explicitly associate observations with time.

options.label: The same failures produce different compliance depending on the time interval considered
options.explanation: Correct — A target percentage is incomplete without defining the population and period over which it is evaluated.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: A request-based availability SLI has 999,000 good events out of 1,000,000 valid events. What is availability?

options.explanation: Correct — The SLI is good events divided by total valid events for the objective window.

options.label: It cannot be computed without CPU utilization
options.explanation: Incorrect — Request availability depends on classified events, not host resource data.
Incorrect — That is the bad-event ratio, not availability.
Incorrect — The supplied counts have one failure per thousand rather than one per ten thousand.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: Why define a latency SLI as “proportion of requests faster than 300 ms” rather than average latency?

options.label: Averages cannot be calculated from numbers
options.explanation: Incorrect — They are calculable but often mask distribution shape.

options.label: It directly measures the fraction of user experiences meeting the stated threshold
options.explanation: Correct — Averages can hide a harmful slow tail while threshold compliance maps cleanly to an SLO.

options.label: Threshold SLIs eliminate the need for histograms
options.explanation: Incorrect — The underlying measurement may still use histogram buckets aligned to the threshold.

options.label: Every user experiences exactly the threshold value
options.explanation: Incorrect — The indicator counts compliance and does not claim identical latencies.

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs

stem: A service with a 1% error budget currently has a 5% bad-event rate. What is its burn rate?

options.explanation: Incorrect — That is the inverse ratio and understates consumption speed.
Incorrect — Subtracting percentages does not calculate normalized budget consumption.
Correct — Burn rate divides observed bad-event rate by the error-budget rate: 5% divided by 1%.
Incorrect — The percentages must be compared as like ratios rather than multiplying by 100 twice.

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs

stem: Why combine a short and long window in an SLO burn-rate alert?

options.label: The short window measures CPU and the long window measures memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — Both windows measure the same SLI budget burn over different durations.

options.label: It doubles the permitted error budget
options.explanation: Incorrect — Windowing changes detection, not the objective’s allowed unreliability.

options.label: Both windows guarantee zero false positives
options.explanation: Incorrect — No alert strategy can guarantee perfect classification under all workloads.

options.label: The long window confirms sustained impact while the short window resets quickly after recovery
options.explanation: Correct — The pair balances sensitivity with stability and avoids alerts lingering solely because of old errors.

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs

stem: Why can percentage-error alerts be noisy for a very low-traffic service?

options.label: One or two failures can create a large ratio from a tiny denominator
options.explanation: Correct — Sparse event counts make proportions volatile and may need minimum-event or longer-window handling.

options.label: Prometheus discards all small numbers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Time-series systems retain small values; the issue is interpretation.

options.label: Percentages cannot represent fewer than 100 requests
options.explanation: Incorrect — Ratios are mathematically defined, but statistical stability is poor at low counts.

options.label: Low traffic always means the service is unavailable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Demand and availability are distinct.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: What makes a page-worthy alert actionable?

options.label: It fires whenever any metric changes
options.explanation: Incorrect — Normal variation would overwhelm responders with unactionable pages.

options.label: It indicates urgent user impact and has a known responder action or investigation path
options.explanation: Correct — Paging should demand timely human intervention rather than merely report interesting state.

options.label: It contains every dashboard panel
options.explanation: Incorrect — An alert needs focused context and runbook guidance, not an exhaustive dashboard dump.

options.label: It can be ignored until business hours
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is better suited to a ticket or report than an urgent page.

stem: What does a Prometheus alert rule’s for duration accomplish?

options.label: Samples older than the duration are deleted
options.explanation: Incorrect — Retention is configured separately from alert pending time.

options.label: The query runs only once at the end
options.explanation: Incorrect — The rule continues evaluation while tracking how long the condition remains true.

options.label: The expression must remain active for that duration before the alert fires
options.explanation: Correct — A pending period filters transient threshold crossings while preserving sustained-condition alerts.

options.label: The alert automatically resolves after that duration
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resolution occurs when the expression stops matching, not simply when time elapses.

stem: During a severe outage, why may rollback precede complete root-cause proof?

options.label: Root causes should never be investigated
options.explanation: Incorrect — Investigation continues after or alongside safe restoration and feeds corrective work.

options.label: Rollback guarantees no data corruption occurred
options.explanation: Incorrect — A rollback can restore code behavior but cannot prove state integrity.

options.label: Every outage is caused by the latest release
options.explanation: Incorrect — Recent changes are useful hypotheses, not universal causes.

options.label: Restoring user service is often lower risk than continuing investigation on the failing version
options.explanation: Correct — Incident response separates immediate mitigation from later causal analysis.

stem: Which postmortem action item is strongest?

options.label: Add bounded queue admission, owned by the API team, due September 1, with a saturation test
options.explanation: Correct — It specifies a concrete system change, owner, deadline, and verification method.

options.label: Never deploy again
options.explanation: Incorrect — Eliminating all change is infeasible and does not address the specific failure mechanism.

options.label: Engineers should be more careful
options.explanation: Incorrect — The statement is neither measurable nor a durable system defense.

options.label: Improve monitoring someday
options.explanation: Incorrect — It lacks scope, owner, priority, deadline, and completion evidence.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: How can a circuit breaker protect a failing dependency?

options.label: It retries every failed call without limit
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unlimited retries increase pressure on the failing dependency.

options.label: After enough failures it fails calls quickly, then probes recovery after a cooldown
options.explanation: Correct — Fail-fast behavior bounds resource use while a half-open phase tests whether normal traffic can resume.

options.label: It permanently disables the dependency after one error
options.explanation: Incorrect — A useful breaker uses thresholds and recovery probing rather than irreversible shutdown.

options.label: It makes downstream responses cacheable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Circuit state controls calls and does not alter HTTP cache directives.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: A frontend has a 1-second deadline and makes two sequential dependencies. Why should each dependency timeout be below one second?

options.label: Shorter timeouts make dependencies execute faster
options.explanation: Incorrect — Timeouts stop waiting but do not accelerate server computation.

options.label: Every dependency must receive exactly half regardless of behavior
options.explanation: Incorrect — Budget allocation should reflect latency distributions, criticality, and remaining time.

options.label: The caller needs time for both work stages, overhead, and a useful response before its own deadline
options.explanation: Correct — Downstream budgets must compose within the end-to-end deadline rather than each consuming all of it.

options.label: A one-second downstream timeout is invalid HTTP
options.explanation: Incorrect — HTTP does not prohibit that value; the problem is deadline composition.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: Why cap retries with a retry budget?

options.label: It replaces per-attempt timeouts
options.explanation: Incorrect — Each attempt still needs a time bound even when total retries are capped.

options.label: It deduplicates non-idempotent writes automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect — Operation semantics and idempotency controls remain separate.

options.label: It guarantees no original request fails
options.explanation: Incorrect — A bounded policy intentionally stops retrying some failures.

options.label: It bounds amplification so retries cannot consume an excessive share of healthy capacity
options.explanation: Correct — A budget allows recovery attempts while protecting the service from retry-driven overload.

stem: Under overload, why classify requests by criticality before shedding?

options.label: The service can preserve high-value or essential operations while rejecting lower-priority work
options.explanation: Correct — Priority-aware admission produces a more useful degraded mode than indiscriminate failure.

options.label: HTTP requires status 200 for high-priority callers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Priority policy does not override truthful response status semantics.

options.label: Priority makes total capacity infinite
options.explanation: Incorrect — Classification allocates scarcity but cannot create compute resources.

options.label: Low-priority requests consume no resources
options.explanation: Incorrect — They still use capacity unless rejected early.

stem: Why bound an in-memory work queue?

options.label: A bound ensures no request is rejected
options.explanation: Incorrect — Once full, a bounded queue must reject or apply backpressure.

options.label: It limits memory and waiting time, allowing overload to surface as controlled rejection
options.explanation: Correct — An unbounded queue converts excess demand into growing latency and eventual process failure.

options.label: It guarantees FIFO is optimal for all work
options.explanation: Incorrect — Queue size and scheduling policy are separate decisions.

options.label: It eliminates downstream latency
options.explanation: Incorrect — The bound controls accumulation but does not speed the dependency.

stem: What is the fairest canary evaluation?

options.label: Compare today’s canary to last year’s fleet average
options.explanation: Incorrect — Workload, dependencies, and seasonality make the historical baseline poorly matched.

options.label: Look only at canary CPU utilization
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resource use alone can miss correctness, latency, and user impact.

options.label: Compare canary and control on contemporaneous, comparable traffic and key outcome metrics
options.explanation: Correct — Parallel cohorts reduce confounding from traffic mix and time-varying conditions.

options.label: Promote if no one reports a complaint in five minutes
options.explanation: Incorrect — Passive complaints are delayed and statistically weak evidence.

stem: A canary’s checkout error rate exceeds control with strong evidence. What is the appropriate next action?

options.label: Hide the error metric from the dashboard
options.explanation: Incorrect — Removing evidence does not restore correctness.

options.label: Immediately delete the previous release artifact
options.explanation: Incorrect — Retaining a known-good rollback target supports fast recovery.

options.label: Increase canary traffic to confirm impact on more users
options.explanation: Incorrect — Once a meaningful guardrail fails, expanding blast radius is unnecessary and harmful.

options.label: Stop promotion and roll back or isolate the canary while investigating
options.explanation: Correct — The canary exists to bound exposure when key guardrails regress.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Testing for Reliability

stem: A fault-injection experiment kills one replica. What must be defined before running it?

options.label: A measurable steady-state hypothesis and an abort condition
options.explanation: Correct — Success criteria and safety bounds turn fault injection into a controlled experiment.

options.label: Permission to affect unlimited production traffic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Safe experiments bound scope and blast radius.

options.label: A guarantee that no monitoring alert can fire
options.explanation: Incorrect — Alerts are useful evidence, and experiments cannot guarantee zero signal change.

options.label: The root cause of a future incident
options.explanation: Incorrect — Experiments test resilience hypotheses rather than predict one exact incident.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Testing for Reliability

stem: Why is successful backup creation insufficient evidence of recoverability?

options.label: Every backup format is inherently invalid
options.explanation: Incorrect — Backups can be reliable, but their recoverability must be demonstrated.

options.label: Backups can be incomplete, corrupt, inaccessible, or too slow to restore until restoration is tested
options.explanation: Correct — Recovery drills validate data integrity, permissions, tooling, and achieved RTO/RPO.

options.label: Restore testing makes future backups unnecessary
options.explanation: Incorrect — New data and system changes require continuing backup and test cycles.

options.label: A restore test guarantees zero future data loss
options.explanation: Incorrect — It provides evidence for a scenario, not certainty against every failure.

stem: Why size a service using peak demand and growth rather than average demand alone?

options.label: Average arithmetic is mathematically undefined for traffic
options.explanation: Incorrect — The average exists but is insufficient for tail demand.

options.label: Peak traffic always persists forever
options.explanation: Incorrect — Peak duration varies; it still matters because saturation can cause rapid failure.

options.label: Average load hides bursts that can saturate queues and violate latency objectives
options.explanation: Correct — Capacity must cover realistic high-demand periods plus failure and growth headroom.

options.label: Growth forecasts eliminate the need for measurement
options.explanation: Incorrect — Forecasts must be updated with observed demand and system benchmarks.

sources.title: Kubernetes: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

stem: A latency-sensitive container hits its CPU limit despite idle CPUs on the node. What can happen?

options.label: The container receives all idle CPU without restriction
options.explanation: Incorrect — A hard CPU quota can prevent use of otherwise idle cycles.

options.label: Only memory latency changes because CPU limits affect RAM
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU throttling directly delays computation and request completion.

options.label: Kubernetes automatically removes the limit
options.explanation: Incorrect — Limits remain configured until workload policy changes.

options.label: It can be throttled and show latency spikes even though node-wide utilization is low
options.explanation: Correct — CPU limits are enforced per cgroup and can constrain runnable work independently of aggregate idle capacity.

sources.title: Kubernetes: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

stem: Why is checking every shared dependency in each pod’s readiness probe dangerous?

options.label: One dependency outage can remove all callers from service, including paths that could still work
options.explanation: Correct — Coupled readiness can amplify a partial dependency failure into total application unavailability.

options.label: Kubernetes ignores readiness failures
options.explanation: Incorrect — Readiness directly controls endpoint participation.

options.label: Readiness probes cannot make network calls
options.explanation: Incorrect — They can, but broad dependency coupling can create systemic failure.

options.label: Dependencies never affect request handling
options.explanation: Incorrect — They often do, but graceful degradation may preserve independent operations.

stem: Why does a PodDisruptionBudget not guarantee availability during a node crash?

options.label: PDBs apply only to Windows containers
options.explanation: Incorrect — They apply to Kubernetes workloads independent of that platform limitation.

options.label: It constrains voluntary evictions, while involuntary disruptions can still remove pods
options.explanation: Correct — Hardware or kernel failure bypasses the eviction budget and requires placement redundancy.

options.label: A PDB controls HTTP status codes rather than pods
options.explanation: Incorrect — It is explicitly a workload disruption policy.

options.label: Node crashes are considered voluntary maintenance
options.explanation: Incorrect — Crashes are involuntary and cannot be prevented by the eviction API.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Load Balancing at the Frontend

stem: Why can least-connections routing outperform round robin when request durations vary widely?

options.label: It guarantees every connection uses equal CPU
options.explanation: Incorrect — Connection count is only a load proxy and work costs can still differ.

options.label: It eliminates health checks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Routing algorithms still need endpoint health and membership information.

options.label: Current connection count approximates outstanding work and avoids repeatedly loading a slow instance
options.explanation: Correct — Round robin ignores heterogeneous request lifetime and can accumulate more work on unlucky backends.

options.label: It preserves client request ordering globally
options.explanation: Incorrect — Distributing across backends does not establish a total request order.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: Why monitor both an external API probe and internal service metrics?

options.label: Both produce identical data and provide redundancy only
options.explanation: Incorrect — They observe different layers and can disagree meaningfully.

options.label: Internal metrics always prove the endpoint is reachable externally
options.explanation: Incorrect — Network, DNS, TLS, and routing failures can occur outside the process.

options.label: External probes expose every internal queue
options.explanation: Incorrect — A remote request sees outcomes, not all implementation state.

options.label: The probe measures user-visible behavior while internal signals help explain causes
options.explanation: Correct — Black-box and white-box views provide complementary symptom and diagnostic evidence.

stem: How can a latency histogram exemplar help an investigator?

options.label: It links a bucket observation to a representative trace context
options.explanation: Correct — Exemplars bridge aggregate metric anomalies to individual trace evidence without labeling every series by trace ID.

options.label: It guarantees the linked trace is the root cause
options.explanation: Incorrect — The trace is an example observation and still requires investigation.

options.label: It changes every bucket into a log message
options.explanation: Incorrect — Exemplars annotate metric points and do not replace the histogram.

options.label: It stores all traces inside the time series
options.explanation: Incorrect — An exemplar carries a small reference rather than full trace payloads.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: Which observation most directly indicates saturation in a bounded worker pool?

options.label: Request traffic is nonzero
options.explanation: Incorrect — Any active service has traffic; nonzero demand alone says nothing about saturation.

options.label: All workers busy while the pending queue and wait time grow
options.explanation: Correct — Demand has reached the processing limit and work is accumulating.

options.label: Disk capacity is 80% allocated but stable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Storage allocation may need planning but does not directly show worker-pool pressure.

options.label: One informational log was emitted
options.explanation: Incorrect — An isolated event lacks evidence of exhausted service capacity.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: What is a useful consequence when a service exhausts its error budget?

options.label: Disable user-facing monitoring
options.explanation: Incorrect — Removing evidence does not restore reliability.

options.label: Permanently stop all feature development
options.explanation: Incorrect — Budgets support an adaptive balance rather than an irreversible freeze.

options.label: Temporarily prioritize reliability work and limit risky changes until performance recovers
options.explanation: Correct — A pre-agreed policy aligns release velocity with measured user reliability.

options.label: Reset the SLO measurement immediately
options.explanation: Incorrect — Changing the window to erase misses destroys the objective’s credibility.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: A recommendation service fails, but checkout does not require recommendations. What is a resilient response?

options.label: Fail every checkout until recommendations recover
options.explanation: Incorrect — That turns a noncritical dependency outage into critical-path unavailability.

options.label: Retry recommendations indefinitely before responding
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unbounded waiting violates latency and can amplify overload.

options.label: Return invented recommendations as if they were fresh
options.explanation: Incorrect — Undisclosed fabricated data can harm correctness and user trust.

options.label: Serve checkout without recommendations and record the degraded dependency outcome
options.explanation: Correct — Optional-feature fallback preserves the critical user journey and supplies diagnostic evidence.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: When can a hedged read reduce tail latency?

options.label: Send a duplicate after a delay to an independent replica and use the first valid response
options.explanation: Correct — A delayed hedge targets rare stragglers while limiting duplicate load compared with immediate duplication.

options.label: Use the same overloaded connection for both attempts
options.explanation: Incorrect — Correlated bottlenecks reduce the chance that the hedge escapes the straggler.

options.label: Hedge every request immediately at any load
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unconditional duplication doubles traffic and can cause the tail problem it tries to solve.

options.label: Send unlimited simultaneous writes and keep all results
options.explanation: Incorrect — Duplicated writes can corrupt semantics and create severe load amplification.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: A scheduled job logs “completed” once per hour. How should monitoring detect that it silently stopped running?

options.label: Alert only when an ERROR log appears
options.explanation: Incorrect — A stopped process cannot emit its own error.

options.label: Alert on absence of the expected completion event within a tolerance window
options.explanation: Correct — The failure produces no error event, so missing expected evidence is the signal.

options.label: Treat no logs as proof of success
options.explanation: Incorrect — Silence is ambiguous and cannot confirm job completion.

options.label: Increase log severity on prior successful runs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Changing old event severity does not detect future absence.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: Which signal best detects messages that exhausted retry policy?

options.label: CPU utilization of one producer
options.explanation: Incorrect — Producer resource use is weak evidence of consumer terminal failures.

options.label: Successful acknowledgment rate with failed messages excluded
options.explanation: Incorrect — Excluding terminal failures can make the system appear healthy.

options.label: Dead-letter queue arrival count and oldest-message age
options.explanation: Correct — Arrivals measure failed processing and age shows whether remediation is keeping up.

options.label: Only the main queue publish count
options.explanation: Incorrect — Ingress does not show which messages exhausted retries.

stem: A load generator waits for each slow response before sending that virtual user’s next request. What latency bias can result?

options.label: Only network latency is measured
options.explanation: Incorrect — End-to-end response time can still be measured, but the sample population is biased.

options.label: Every measured latency is multiplied twice
options.explanation: Incorrect — The bias comes from missing scheduled requests, not arithmetic duplication.

options.label: The test always overloads the service
options.explanation: Incorrect — Waiting reduces pressure during stalls and can hide overload.

options.label: Coordinated omission underreports requests that would have arrived during stalls
options.explanation: Correct — The generator reduces offered load exactly when the service is slow, omitting waiting experiences present in an open arrival process.

stem: A team adds trace_id as a metric label. What failure mode is most likely?

options.label: Nearly every observation creates a new time series, overwhelming ingestion and storage
options.explanation: Correct — Trace identifiers are intentionally unique and therefore disastrous as metric dimensions.

options.label: All traces merge into one series
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unique identifiers split rather than merge label sets.

options.label: Metric values become cryptographically signed
options.explanation: Incorrect — A label changes series identity and provides no authenticity.

options.label: Prometheus automatically moves the label into exemplars
options.explanation: Incorrect — Backends do not silently reinterpret arbitrary high-cardinality labels.

stem: Why is averaging the p99 values from ten Prometheus summaries mathematically invalid?

options.label: A percentile can never be computed from any telemetry
options.explanation: Incorrect — It can be estimated correctly from an aggregate distribution.

options.label: Quantiles do not compose; each p99 describes a different local distribution and request count
options.explanation: Correct — A fleet percentile requires aggregatable observations such as shared histogram buckets.

options.label: Summaries expose only counters
options.explanation: Incorrect — They expose quantile samples plus sum and count, but client-calculated quantiles are not aggregatable.

options.label: Ten is below the minimum number of instances
options.explanation: Incorrect — The mathematical problem exists for any number greater than one.

stem: When computing a quantile from classic histogram counters that can reset, why apply rate before summing by bucket boundary?

options.label: Sum cannot operate on metric samples
options.explanation: Incorrect — PromQL sum is valid; the order matters for reset handling.

options.label: Quantiles require raw logs rather than buckets
options.explanation: Incorrect — Histogram quantiles are specifically estimated from bucket series.

options.label: Rate detects resets per original series before aggregation hides them
