options.explanation: Correct — Summing counters first can mask a reset when other instances continue increasing.

options.label: Bucket boundaries change after rate is applied
options.explanation: Incorrect — Rate transforms values over time but leaves label boundaries intact.

stem: Why should trace IDs be generated with high-quality randomness rather than sequential values?

options.label: Sequential IDs force every span to be a root
options.explanation: Incorrect — Parentage is represented separately by parent identifiers.

options.label: Sequential IDs cannot be represented in hexadecimal
options.explanation: Incorrect — They can be encoded, but predictability and distribution remain problematic.

options.label: Random IDs encrypt the trace payload
options.explanation: Incorrect — Identifier randomness does not provide telemetry confidentiality.

options.label: Random IDs reduce collision risk and make sampling decisions statistically uniform and less predictable
options.explanation: Correct — W3C guidance relies on globally unique, uniformly distributed identifiers for interoperability and sampling.

stem: A vendor mutates its entry in tracestate. Where should that entry be placed?

options.label: At the beginning of the list
options.explanation: Correct — List order conveys recency, so a mutating system moves its key to the leftmost position.

options.label: At the end to preserve oldest-first ordering
options.explanation: Incorrect — The specification uses leftmost as the most recently updated position.

options.label: In traceparent after the trace flags
options.explanation: Incorrect — Vendor state belongs in tracestate and cannot extend traceparent arbitrarily.

options.label: In the request body only
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trace context must propagate independently of application payload format.

stem: Why should sampled trace counts not be used directly as exact request-rate metrics?

options.label: Traces contain no timestamps
options.explanation: Incorrect — Spans have start and end timestamps, but sampling still biases counts.

options.label: Sampling can be nonuniform and outcome-aware, so retained traces are not necessarily a representative count
options.explanation: Correct — Metrics aggregate all events through defined instruments, whereas traces may be intentionally biased toward interesting cases.

options.label: Every trace represents exactly ten requests
options.explanation: Incorrect — A trace normally follows one distributed transaction, without a fixed sampling multiplier.

options.label: Metrics cannot count requests either
options.explanation: Incorrect — Counters are designed to count events accurately within their collection semantics.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: A request fails both latency and correctness criteria. In a request-based SLI, how should the total and bad-event counts be designed?

options.label: Count it as good if either criterion passed
options.explanation: Incorrect — An AND-defined good event fails when any required criterion is missed.

options.label: Count it twice in total because two symptoms occurred
options.explanation: Incorrect — Duplicating denominator events changes the population and distorts availability.

options.label: Count one eligible request once, with the event classified bad if it violates the defined good criteria
options.explanation: Correct — Mutually consistent event accounting prevents one request from consuming the denominator or budget multiple times unintentionally.

options.label: Exclude it because classification is ambiguous
options.explanation: Incorrect — The SLI should define combined good criteria rather than discard severe failures.

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs

stem: A 14.4x burn-rate alert uses a one-hour long window. Roughly what does that threshold mean for a 30-day budget?

options.label: The budget is exhausted in 14.4 hours
options.explanation: Incorrect — Burn rate is a multiplier, not directly the remaining lifetime in hours.

options.label: Exactly 14.4% of requests are failing
options.explanation: Incorrect — Burn rate is normalized by the allowed error rate and is not the raw failure percentage.

options.label: The service has 50 hours of downtime remaining
options.explanation: Incorrect — The calculation describes equivalent budget consumption, not necessarily contiguous downtime.

options.label: At sustained burn, the entire budget would be consumed in about 50 hours
options.explanation: Correct — Budget lifetime is the objective window divided by burn rate: 720 hours divided by 14.4.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: A team changes the definition of a “valid request” midway through an SLO window. What is required for a defensible trend?

options.label: Version the SLI and recompute comparable history or clearly mark the discontinuity
options.explanation: Correct — Changing numerator or denominator semantics breaks direct comparison unless historical data is reclassified.

options.label: Silently splice the new series into the old dashboard
options.explanation: Incorrect — An unmarked semantic change creates misleading apparent improvement or regression.

options.label: Reset all production counters on every host
options.explanation: Incorrect — Counter resets do not make the underlying event definitions comparable.

options.label: Keep the old target but discard the denominator
options.explanation: Incorrect — A percentage objective requires a well-defined population.

stem: A proposed label has 100 methods, 50 regions, and 1,000 tenants. What worst-case series multiplier does it add per base metric?

options.label: Exactly one because labels share a metric name
options.explanation: Incorrect — Distinct label sets define distinct time series despite the shared metric name.

options.label: Five million label combinations
options.explanation: Correct — Independent cardinalities multiply: 100 times 50 times 1,000.

options.label: 1,150 combinations
options.explanation: Incorrect — Adding cardinalities understates the Cartesian product of label sets.

options.label: 100,000 combinations
options.explanation: Incorrect — This omits the region dimension from the multiplication.

stem: Why should an incident commander limit simultaneous uncoordinated mitigations?

options.label: Only one engineer may ever access production
options.explanation: Incorrect — Access can be distributed safely when roles and actions are coordinated.

options.label: Parallel work is always slower
options.explanation: Incorrect — Independent investigation can be parallel; risky state changes need control.

options.label: Multiple changes obscure causality and can interact, making recovery state harder to assess or reverse
options.explanation: Correct — Serialized or explicitly coordinated actions preserve an understandable timeline and rollback path.

options.label: Monitoring cannot observe more than one change
options.explanation: Incorrect — Telemetry can observe them, but attribution becomes substantially harder.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Testing for Reliability

stem: A region failover succeeds, but the team has never tested returning traffic to the primary. What risk remains?

options.label: The secondary must now remain primary forever
options.explanation: Incorrect — A tested failback plan allows restoration when conditions permit.

options.label: RPO becomes zero automatically after failover
options.explanation: Incorrect — Data-loss tolerance depends on replication and recovery points, not role naming.

options.label: Successful failover proves every reverse step
options.explanation: Incorrect — Direction-dependent replication and routing make that inference unsafe.

options.label: Failback can encounter divergent state, stale configuration, or capacity transients not exercised by failover
options.explanation: Correct — Recovery is bidirectional; restoring normal topology is a distinct operation requiring rehearsal.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Testing for Reliability

stem: Production data and backups use credentials and storage in the same failure domain. What design weakness exists?

options.label: A single compromise or regional failure can destroy both primary and recovery copies
options.explanation: Correct — Independent access controls and fault domains are necessary for credible disaster recovery.

options.label: The RTO is guaranteed to be zero
options.explanation: Incorrect — Shared failure domains do not make restoration instantaneous.

options.label: Backups will always restore faster
options.explanation: Incorrect — Co-location may reduce latency but increases correlated-loss risk.

options.label: Encryption becomes impossible
options.explanation: Incorrect — Encryption is possible, though key separation also matters.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: Five service layers each retry three times. What systemic risk arises?

options.label: Retries collapse into exactly three total attempts
options.explanation: Incorrect — Without coordination, each layer can multiply attempts from the layer above.

options.label: One user request can expand into hundreds of downstream attempts
options.explanation: Correct — Multiplicative retries across layers amplify load dramatically during dependency failure.

options.label: The deepest service receives fewer calls than normal
options.explanation: Incorrect — Layered retries increase rather than reduce offered calls.

options.label: Every attempt is automatically deduplicated
options.explanation: Incorrect — Deduplication requires explicit operation identity and server behavior.

stem: Why can adaptive concurrency limiting react better than a fixed high limit?

options.label: It predicts every future traffic spike exactly
options.explanation: Incorrect — Adaptive control responds to observations and does not provide perfect forecasting.

options.label: It guarantees maximum throughput with zero latency
options.explanation: Incorrect — Throughput and latency remain constrained by service capacity.

options.label: It lowers admitted work when latency signals saturation and cautiously raises it when capacity recovers
options.explanation: Correct — Feedback control follows changing dependency capacity and avoids persistent queue overload.

options.label: It removes the need for an admission queue bound
options.explanation: Incorrect — Multiple overload controls remain complementary.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

stem: How should a service constrain hedged requests during overload?

options.label: Hedge writes without idempotency controls
options.explanation: Incorrect — Duplicate mutation can create inconsistent or repeated effects.

options.label: Ignore cancellation after one hedge wins
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cancelling losing work promptly returns capacity to the system.

options.label: Immediately duplicate every request to every replica
options.explanation: Incorrect — This maximizes amplification and can collapse the entire replica set.

options.label: Use a small hedge budget and delay based on normal latency, disabling hedges when capacity is scarce
options.explanation: Correct — Bounded selective duplication targets stragglers without turning overload into doubled demand.

stem: A canary receives 100 requests and no errors while the baseline error rate is 0.1%. What can be concluded?

options.label: The sample is too small to show that the canary preserves such a low error rate with confidence
options.explanation: Correct — Zero observed failures is plausible even for materially worse low rates at this sample size.

options.label: Statistical reasoning is unnecessary for deployments
options.explanation: Incorrect — Traffic volume and expected rates determine whether observed differences are meaningful.

options.label: The canary is proven error-free
options.explanation: Incorrect — Absence of observed failures is not proof of a zero underlying rate.

options.label: The canary is exactly ten times better
options.explanation: Incorrect — There is insufficient evidence for a precise comparative effect.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

stem: All synthetic probes run inside the same cloud region as the service. What blind spot remains?

options.label: Internal probes cannot make HTTP requests
options.explanation: Incorrect — They can test HTTP but from a limited vantage point.

options.label: External DNS, routing, or regional reachability failures may be invisible
options.explanation: Correct — Shared network fate can let internal probes succeed while real users elsewhere cannot connect.

options.label: Application correctness is fully proven by local reachability
options.explanation: Incorrect — A successful probe covers only its scripted path and location.

options.label: More frequent local probes eliminate geographic bias
options.explanation: Incorrect — Frequency does not add independent network vantage points.

stem: Why must all spans of a trace reach the same stateful tail-sampling decision point?

options.label: Span IDs are valid only on one machine
options.explanation: Incorrect — Identifiers are designed for distributed propagation.

options.label: Collectors cannot forward telemetry over networks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Collectors commonly receive and route remote telemetry.

options.label: The sampler needs a coherent view of the trace outcome before choosing keep or drop
options.explanation: Correct — Partitioning one trace across independent samplers can produce incomplete decisions and partial exports.

options.label: Head sampling requires the same arrangement
options.explanation: Incorrect — Head decisions are made early and propagated, so they do not require buffering every span centrally.

stem: A child span appears to start before its remote parent because host clocks differ. What should analysis avoid?

options.label: Collecting duration measurements
options.explanation: Incorrect — Monotonic local duration can remain useful despite wall-clock skew.

options.label: Recording the anomaly for clock-health investigation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Large skew is useful operational evidence and can be monitored.

options.label: Using parent and span identifiers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Those identifiers are precisely what preserve causal linkage across hosts.

options.label: Inferring causal reversal solely from wall-clock timestamps
options.explanation: Correct — Trace parentage supplies causal structure, while unsynchronized clocks can distort absolute span timing.

stem: An API writes an unsanitized username directly into line-oriented logs. What attack can newline characters enable?

options.label: Log injection that creates forged entries or disrupts downstream parsing
options.explanation: Correct — Control characters can break record boundaries and make attacker text appear as trusted events.

options.label: Metric counter overflow only
options.explanation: Incorrect — The primary issue is forged or malformed log records, not numeric counters.

options.label: Automatic privilege escalation in the operating system
options.explanation: Incorrect — Log injection affects audit integrity and tools, not inherently OS permissions.

options.label: TLS certificate renewal
options.explanation: Incorrect — Log content has no certificate-lifecycle authority.

stem: An alert rule groups by request_id. Why can this harm incident response?

options.label: Grouping always removes all alert context
options.explanation: Incorrect — Grouping can preserve useful bounded dimensions; request ID is the problematic choice.

options.label: It creates one alert instance per request, overwhelming storage, routing, and responders
options.explanation: Correct — Unique identifiers turn a single condition into an unbounded alert cardinality explosion.

options.label: Request IDs are required to be constant
options.explanation: Incorrect — They are intentionally unique across requests.

options.label: Alert managers cannot route labels
options.explanation: Incorrect — Routing is label-based, which makes excessive unique label sets especially costly.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives

stem: A dependency’s SLO equals your product SLO, and every product request requires it. Why is this risky?

options.label: Equal SLOs mathematically multiply to 100%
options.explanation: Incorrect — Serial availability does not improve through multiplication.

options.label: The product inherits unused dependency budget automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect — Separate services cannot transfer reliability allowance this way.

options.label: The dependency alone can consume the entire product error budget, leaving no allowance for your own failures
options.explanation: Correct — A product generally needs dependencies substantially more reliable or needs redundancy and degradation paths.

options.label: Your own code can no longer fail
options.explanation: Incorrect — Application and dependency failures remain independent contributors.

stem: A three-zone service must survive losing one zone without overload. What capacity condition is required?

options.label: Each zone should run near 100% before failure
options.explanation: Incorrect — Then any failure immediately exceeds remaining capacity.

options.label: Autoscaling guarantees instant replacement in another zone
options.explanation: Incorrect — Scaling has detection, provisioning, warm-up, and quota delays and cannot replace baseline resilience.

options.label: Normal fleet capacity need only equal average traffic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Average sizing leaves no room for peaks or zone loss.

options.label: The remaining two zones together must carry peak load with operational headroom
options.explanation: Correct — Failure planning must test capacity after removing the largest required fault domain.
